issues.legal_issue: The time limit for commencing an estate-duty first assessment applies to all proceedings for its levy, including assessment proceedings.
material_facts: The deceased’s estate had not been reported or assessed within five years of the death.
After that period had expired, the appellant filed a return and the estate-duty authority issued a notice seeking information and initiating assessment proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The authority could not commence estate-duty assessment proceedings after the five-year limit had expired; the term “levy” includes assessment and imposition of duty.
issues.legal_principle: Section 73A of the Estate Duty Act, 1953 imposes an imperative, comprehensive bar on commencing proceedings for levy after the applicable period. “Levy” includes assessment and imposition of tax, as explained in Padampat Singhania v. Controller of Estate Duty, Kanpur, drawing on Assistant Collector of Central Excise v. National Tobacco Co. of India Ltd. The Court approved Controller of Estate Duty v. Bhola Dutt and distinguished P.C. Saxena v. The State.

predicates.first_estate_duty_assessment: The proceeding concerns the first assessment of estate duty on a deceased person’s estate.
predicates.limitation_period_elapsed: The prescribed time for commencing that first assessment had expired before the authority began proceedings.

issues.definition: When a first estate-duty assessment is begun after the prescribed time has expired, the assessment proceedings are barred.

issues.legal_issue: An applicant for a succession certificate need not produce a duty-clearance certificate that the estate-duty authority is barred from issuing because the time to commence assessment proceedings has expired.
material_facts: The appellant applied for a succession certificate after attaining majority.
No account or return for the estate had been filed within five years of the deceased’s death.
The civil court required a certificate from the estate-duty authority, and the authority later initiated assessment proceedings after the five-year period had expired.
issues.conclusion: Requiring the appellant to produce a certificate that the authority could not issue because of the statutory bar would demand impossible compliance; Section 56 must be read consistently with that bar.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 56 and 73A of the Estate Duty Act, 1953 must be read harmoniously: the requirement to produce a duty-clearance certificate does not permit assessment proceedings to be commenced after the time limit has expired. The Court applied the interpretive principle that statutory meaning should reflect the enactment’s intent rather than adhere mechanically to its letter, citing Herbert Broom’s Legal Maxims. It treated P.C. Saxena v. The State as establishing that a civil court could not itself waive the certificate condition, not as authority that the time bar was inapplicable.

rule.if: succession_certificate_application and first_assessment_case and limitation_period_elapsed and clearance_certificate_unavailable

predicates.succession_certificate_application: An applicant sought a succession certificate from a civil court.
predicates.first_assessment_case: The estate-duty matter concerns a first assessment of the deceased’s estate.
predicates.limitation_period_elapsed: The prescribed time for commencing the first assessment had expired.
predicates.clearance_certificate_unavailable: The estate-duty authority could not issue a clearance certificate because it could no longer commence the assessment proceedings.

issues.definition: When a succession-certificate application concerns a first assessment whose time limit has expired and the required clearance is unavailable for that reason, the applicant need not produce that unobtainable clearance.
